title: Ambhasy apāre: the one beyond the waters, the gāyatrīs of the gods, and the mantras of the bath
theme: A hymn to the one beyond the waters, from whom time, the worlds and all creatures come and who is grasped only by the heart; then twelve short gāyatrīs addressed to the gods; then the mantras said over dūrvā grass and earth, in the water, under it and after the bath, ending with the bather’s words ‘I am brahman’.

translation.literal: Greater than the great — on the far shore of the waters, in the middle of the world, on the back of the vault of heaven — having fully entered the lights with [his] brightness, Prajāpati moves within the womb. In which all this comes together and goes apart, in which all the gods have settled: that indeed is what has been, that also what is to be, ah, this [too]; that [rests] in the imperishable, in the highest space. By which space and heaven and earth are covered, by which the sun shines with heat and radiance; whom the seers weave within the ocean; which [is] in the imperishable, the highest — [it brings forth] the creatures. From which the bringing forth of the world came; [which] with water let loose living beings on the earth; which by the plants entered men and animals, the beings moving and unmoving. Than this nothing else is higher or subtler; which [is] higher than the high, greater than the great; which [is] one, unmanifest, of endless form, all, ancient, beyond darkness.
translation.readable: Greater than the greatest things — beyond the farthest shore of the ocean, at the centre of the world, above the vault of heaven — the lord of creatures moves within the cosmic womb, having entered every light with his own. In him all this gathers and disperses; in him all the gods are seated. He is what has been and what is to be, and this present world too, resting in the imperishable, the highest space. He covers sky, heaven and earth; by him the sun burns and shines; the seers weave him through the ocean of the world. From him came the birth of the world; by water he set living beings on the earth, and as food he entered men, animals and all that moves and does not move. Nothing is higher or subtler than he: higher than the high, greater than the great, one, unmanifest, of endless form, the whole, the ancient, beyond darkness.

translation.literal: That indeed they call right order, that also truth; that indeed [is] brahman, the highest of the seers. The navel of the world bears sacrifice and public works, the world born in many ways and being born. That indeed [is] fire, that wind, that the sun, that also the moon; that indeed [is] the bright, the immortal; that brahman, that the waters, he Prajāpati. All the blinks were born from the lightning-like Person; kalās, muhūrtas, kāṣṭhās, days and nights, all together; half-months, months, seasons and the year — let them be arranged. He milked out the waters, these two, the mid-region and heaven. No one has grasped him above, nor across, nor in the middle; no one rules over him; his name [is] great glory.
translation.readable: They call it right order and they call it truth; it is brahman, the highest thing the seers know. As the hub of the world it bears the whole world, born in so many ways and still being born, and all its sacrifices and good works. It is fire, wind, sun and moon; it is the shining and the immortal; it is brahman, the waters and the lord of creatures. From that shining Person every instant of time was born — the smallest moments, the hours, days and nights, fortnights, months, seasons and the year. He drew sustenance from the waters and from both regions above. No one has ever grasped him — not above, not across, not in the middle. No one rules him. His very name is great glory.

translation.literal: His form does not stand within sight; no one sees him with the eye. Grasped by the heart, by the master of thought, by the mind — those who know him become immortal. ‘From the waters born’; ‘the golden embryo’ — [these] eight. This god indeed [is in] all the quarters; first born indeed, he also [is] within the womb. He, being born; he, to be born; facing inward he stands, facing every way: with eyes everywhere and faces everywhere, hands everywhere and feet everywhere. With his two arms he welds together, with wings together, producing heaven and earth, the one god. Vena, seeing that, knowing all the worlds — where all becomes one nest; in which this [comes] together and apart, the one; he, woven along and across, pervading creatures — the gandharva by name, knowing, proclaimed that immortal, hidden in the caves.
translation.readable: His form is not within sight; no eye has ever seen him. He is grasped by the heart, by the mind turned inward; those who know him become immortal. [Here the recitation adds two passages known by their opening words: the anuvāka ‘born from the waters’ and the eight verses of the hymn to the Golden Embryo.] This god is in every quarter. He was born first, and he is within the womb; he is what is being born and what will be born; he stands within all and faces every way, with eyes, faces, hands and feet on every side. The one god brings forth heaven and earth, welding them together with his arms and wings. The gandharva Vena saw that in which the whole world becomes a single nest, in which all this comes together and comes apart, the one that is woven through creatures lengthwise and across; knowing all the worlds, he proclaimed that immortal thing hidden in the cave of the heart.

translation.literal: Three steps are placed in the caves; who knows that becomes the father of the begetter. He [is] our kinsman, the begetter, he the ordainer; he knows the abodes, all the worlds — where the gods, having attained immortality, reached the abodes in the third [world]. They go around heaven and earth at once, around the worlds, around the quarters, around heaven. Having unravelled the stretched thread of right order, he saw that, he became that among creatures. Having gone round the worlds, round the beings, round all the quarters and directions, Prajāpati, the first-born of right order, by himself became one with the self. The wondrous lord of the seat, dear to Indra, desirable, gain [and] intelligence I have obtained. Blaze up, Jātavedas, striking away my destruction.
translation.readable: Three states lie hidden in the cave of the heart; whoever knows them becomes father even to his own father. He is our kinsman and our begetter; he orders all things and knows every abode and every world, where the gods, having won immortality, reached their places in the third heaven. Those who know go at once around heaven and earth, around the worlds, the directions and the sky. One who has unwound the long thread of truth and seen it becomes that, among all creatures. Prajāpati, first-born of truth, went round the worlds, the beings and all the directions, and by his own self became one with the self. I have come to the wondrous lord of the seat, dear to Indra, longed for by all; I have gained his gifts and intelligence. Blaze up, Agni, and strike away my ruin.

translation.literal: So multiply us, dūrvā, by a thousand and a hundred — you who spread out by a hundred and sprout by a thousand: to that one, to you, goddess Iṣṭakā, may we offer with an offering. O [earth] trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, trodden by Viṣṇu, bearer of wealth: I shall bear you on my head; protect me at every step. Earth, a cow, the bearer, the bearer of worlds — you were lifted up by the black hundred-armed Boar. O earth, destroy my sin, the wrong done by me. O earth, you are given by Brahmā, consecrated by Kāśyapa. O earth, give me nourishment; in you all is established.
translation.readable: As you spread by hundreds and grow by thousands, dūrvā, so make us spread by hundreds and thousands. Goddess, we honour you with an offering. [Over the earth taken for the bath:] Earth, walked on by horses, by chariots and by Viṣṇu’s stride, bearer of all wealth — I shall carry you on my head; protect me at every step. You are the earth, a giving cow, the bearer of all the worlds, lifted out of the flood by the great black Boar of a hundred arms. Earth, destroy the wrong I have done. You were given by Brahmā and consecrated by Kāśyapa. Earth, give me strength; in you everything is established.

translation.literal: O earth, O firm ground, drive out all that [sin] of mine, O earth. By that [sin] being slain I go to the highest goal. From what we fear, Indra, from that make safety for us. Bountiful one, help — that [power] of yours for our protection; strike down the haters, the assailants. Giver of well-being, lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, subduer of assailants, the bull Indra — may he go before us, giver of well-being, maker of safety. Well-being for us — Indra of increased fame; well-being for us — Pūṣan who possesses all; well-being for us — Tārkṣya with unharmed wheel-rim; well-being for us may Bṛhaspati grant. Of quick anger, swift in striking, roaring, vigorous, armed with arrows, possessing the soma-dregs, Soma [crushed] all the brushwood and trees; the counterparts on this side did not harm Indra.
translation.readable: Earth, firm ground of all beings, drive out all my wrongdoing; with that wrong destroyed, I go to the highest goal. Indra, give us safety from whatever we fear. Bountiful one, use your power to protect us; strike down those who hate and attack us. May Indra go before us — giver of well-being, lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, master of all assailants, the rain-giving bull, maker of safety. May Indra of great fame, Pūṣan who owns all things, Garuḍa whose course nothing harms, and Bṛhaspati give us well-being. [A verse of the Ṛgveda:] Fierce, swift to strike, roaring, mighty, armed and strong with soma, Soma swept through the forests; no rival on earth has ever matched Indra.

translation.literal: Brahman, born first in the east, the lovely one, uncovered the bright [worlds] from the boundary; he uncovered the deep ones, the near ones, the abodes of this [world], the source of the existent and of the non-existent. Be kind, O earth, bringer forth of men, giver of dwelling; grant us shelter, [you who are] broad. Her whose sign is fragrance, hard to assail, ever nourished, rich in cattle, mistress of all beings — that Śrī I call here. May Śrī come to me; may my misfortune perish. The gods led by Viṣṇu indeed won these worlds with the metres, so that they could not be won back. May the great Indra, thunderbolt-armed, of sixteen parts, grant shelter.
translation.readable: Brahman, born first in the east and longed for by all, opened up the shining worlds from their bounds, and laid open the deep quarters near at hand, the dwellings of this world, the source of what is and of what is not. Be kind to us, Earth; you bring forth people and give them a place to live; give us shelter, wide one. [Over the earth taken for the bath:] I call here Śrī, known by her fragrance, unshakeable, ever-nourished, rich in cattle, mistress of all beings. May fortune come to me; may misfortune leave me. The gods, led by Viṣṇu, won these worlds with the metres, never to be won back. May great Indra, thunderbolt in hand, full like the sixteen-digit moon, give us shelter.

translation.literal: May the bountiful one make well-being for us; may he strike the evil that hates us. Make [me] a presser of soma, one who sounds [the hymns], O lord of brahman — [as] Kakṣīvant, who [was] Uśij’s son. The body, defilement of the sacrifice, [is] a base place: in it may he sink who hates us. The foot [is] a purifier, outstretched, ancient, purified by which one crosses wrongdoings: purified by that pure purifier, may we cross over evil, the enemy. In accord, Indra, with your troop, with the Maruts, drink the soma, slayer of Vṛtra, hero, knowing; strike the enemies, push away the attackers; then make safety for us on all sides. May the waters and plants be good friends to us; may they be bad friends to him who hates us and whom we hate. Waters, you are bringers of joy: set us towards strength.
translation.readable: May Indra give us well-being and strike down the evil that hates us. Lord of the Veda, make me one who presses soma and sounds the hymns, as you made Kakṣīvant, son of Uśij. Let the one who hates us sink into what is base. [Standing knee-deep in the water:] Viṣṇu’s foot is a purifier, outstretched and ancient; purified by it a man crosses beyond his wrongs — purified by that pure purifier, may we cross beyond evil, our enemy. Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, hero, come with the Maruts and drink the soma; strike our enemies, drive off our attackers and give us safety on every side. [Standing navel-deep:] May the waters and the plants be friends to us, and unfriendly to whoever hates us and whom we hate. Waters, you bring joy: give us strength.

translation.literal: For the great, for delight, for seeing. That most auspicious essence of yours — give us a share of it here, like loving mothers. For that let us go readily to you, for whose dwelling you quicken [us]; and, waters, make us generate. I approach golden-horned Varuṇa for refuge; give me a ford, being asked. What I have eaten of the bad, and acceptance from sinners, what wrong I have done by mind, speech or deed — that of ours may Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ purify again and again. Homage to Agni who dwells in the waters, homage to Indra, homage to Varuṇa, homage to Vāruṇī, homage to the waters.
translation.readable: — for greatness, for joy, for the vision [of the highest]. Like loving mothers, give us here a share of your most blessed essence. For that we come gladly to you, waters, who are pleased to destroy our wrongs; make us fruitful. I take refuge in Varuṇa, whose crown is golden; you whom I ask, give me a place to bathe. Whatever I have eaten in the houses of the wicked, whatever gifts I have taken from sinners, whatever wrong I have done in thought, word or deed — may Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ purify it, again and again. Homage to Agni hidden in the waters, to Indra, to Varuṇa, to Varuṇa’s consort, and to the waters.

The commentator reads abhīddha as the all-shining Supreme («सर्वतो देदीप्यामानः परमात्मा») and tapas as reflection, from which right order and truth were born. These three verses are the aghamarṣaṇa, said while immersed in the water («जले निमग्नस्य प्राणायामार्थमघमर्षणसूक्तमाह»).

translation.literal: Whatever of the waters is harmful, whatever impure, whatever unsettling — let that go away. From eating too much, from drinking too much, and what [comes] from accepting from the fierce — that of ours may Varuṇa the king wipe away with his hand. I, then, sinless, stainless, released, freed of guilt, having climbed the summit of heaven, would go to sharing a world with Brahman. And Varuṇa who is in the waters — may he, the wiper-away of sin, purify. Attend to this praise of mine, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, with Paruṣṇī; hear, Marudvṛdhā with Asiknī, Ārjīkīyā with Vitastā and Suṣomā. Right order and truth were born from the kindled heat; from that night was born, from that the ocean, the flood.
translation.readable: Let whatever in the waters is harmful, unclean or disturbing go away. Whatever wrong comes of eating or drinking too much, or of taking gifts from dangerous people, may King Varuṇa wipe it away with his own hand. Then, sinless, stainless, set free and rid of guilt, I would climb to the summit of heaven and reach the world of Brahman. May Varuṇa, who dwells in the waters, the remover of sin, purify me. [The rivers invoked:] Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, Paruṣṇī; Asiknī, Marudvṛdhā, Vitastā, Ārjīkīyā, Suṣomā — come and hear my praise. [The aghamarṣaṇa, said under the water:] From the blazing heat of reflection right order and truth were born; from it the night, from it the billowing ocean.

translation.literal: From the ocean, from the flood, the year was born, ordaining days and nights, master of all that blinks. The creator fashioned sun and moon as before, and heaven and earth, and the mid-region, and also the world of light. Whatever stain of our own [is] on earth, in the mid-region, in heaven and earth — may Varuṇa, the waters, the remover of sin, purify these [of] that. May the Vasus purify, may Varuṇa purify, may Aghamarṣaṇa purify. He in the midst of what has been, the guardian of the world; he [gives] the worlds of the doers of good; he [gives] the golden [world] of death; the golden heaven resting between heaven and earth —
translation.readable: From the ocean was born the year, which orders days and nights and rules all that lives. The creator made the sun and moon as before, and heaven, earth, the mid-region and the world of light. [After the aghamarṣaṇa, while bathing:] Whatever stain is ours, on earth, in the mid-region or between heaven and earth, may Varuṇa, who is the waters and removes sin, wash it from us. May the Vasus purify us; may Varuṇa purify us; may Aghamarṣaṇa purify us. He is the guardian of all that has been and of the world; he grants the worlds of those who do good; he holds the golden world of death; and the golden heaven that rests between heaven and earth —

Vedic aorist of √kram; the base prints it with long ā. The commentator glosses ‘has pervaded’.
The commentator gives a second, Śaiva reading of soma in this verse: ‘with Umā’ (sa + umā), Umā standing for the knowledge of brahman («तयोमया सह विद्यमानत्वात्सोमः»).

translation.literal: — that heaven grant to us. The moist blazes; I am the light. The light blazes; I am brahman. I who am — I am brahman. I am — I am brahman. I myself, I offer myself: svāhā. One who does what must not be done, who has broken his vow, a thief, a slayer of an embryo, a violator of the teacher’s bed — [by] Varuṇa of the waters, the remover of sin, [he] is released from that sin. ‘I am a ground of impurity; do [not] make me weep’ — so the wise declare. The ocean has strode over [all], bringing forth creatures at the first dispensation, the king of the world. The bull, on the filter, on the woollen ridge, has grown greatly — Soma, the drop, being pressed.
translation.readable: — grant us that heaven. [Sipping water after the bath:] This water shines; I am that light. The light shines; I am brahman. I who am — I am brahman. I am — I am brahman. I offer myself, in myself: svāhā. Whoever has done what is forbidden, broken his vow, stolen, killed, or violated his teacher’s bed is freed from that sin by Varuṇa, lord of the waters, the remover of wrong. [For hidden wrongs:] ‘I am a ground of impurity — do not make me weep,’ the wise say. The ocean has filled all things, the king of the world, bringing forth creatures at the first ordering of things. The bull has grown great on the woollen filter, on the summit — Soma, the pressed drop.

syntax: The anuvāka is a chain of separate mantras, not one sentence. Units 10.1.1–10.1.4 are hymn verses about the highest in the third person, built on relative clauses (yasmin … yena … yataḥ … yat) and on refrains (tad eva … tad u …; na … na …). Two pratīkas, ‘adbhyaḥ sambhūtaḥ’ and ‘hiraṇyagarbha ityaṣṭau’, stand for passages recited in full at that point. 10.1.4–10.1.5 turn to Agni with imperatives (uddīpyasva, āvaha, mā hiṃsīt). The twelve gāyatrīs share one frame: X vidmahe, Y dhīmahi, tan no Z pracodayāt — ‘we know X, we meditate on Y; may Z impel us to that’, the names standing in the dative where the sense is accusative. The bath mantras (from 10.1.7) address dūrvā, the earth, Indra, the waters and Varuṇa in the vocative with imperatives (haratu, hana, dehi, nuda, kṛdhi, punantu), and close in the first person (aham asmi, juhomi).

ambiguities.note: The base reads prasūtā … prasūtī; the anonymous commentator reads the second word as prasūtiḥ, ‘the birth of the world’, with prasūtā agreeing with it. The padaccheda follows him. His gloss also allows the reading vyasasarja for vyacasarja, explained the same way.

Printed as one plural word, ‘facing inward’, beside a singular verb. The anonymous commentator divides it: pratyaṅ, ‘the inner one’, within the sheaths of food and the rest («प्रत्यङ्ङन्नमयादिकोशेभ्य आन्तरः»), and mukhāḥ, ‘the chief’, as overseer of body and senses. The padaccheda keeps the printed word.

The Ṛgveda verse (RV 1.22.15) is usually divided bhava anṛkṣarā, ‘without thorns’; the anonymous commentator divides bhavā nṛkṣarā and explains nṛkṣarā from nṛ, ‘people’. The padaccheda follows the commentator and says so.

An epithet of Agni Vaiśvānara found nowhere else in the sources, and the witnesses differ near it. The anonymous commentator takes it as helā-līla, ‘whose sport is play’, the h lost, and also offers the division vaiśvānarāya vidma helālīlāya; both are his suggestions.
As printed the line says ‘make me weep’. The anonymous commentator reads tva as tvam and supplies a negative, ‘do not make me weep’; the translation marks the supplied word.

The closing Ṛgvedic verse speaks of Soma pressed on the woollen filter. The anonymous commentator also reads soma as sa-umā, ‘with Umā’, and the ridge as the lotus of the heart; that is his reading, not the verse’s plain sense.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Several metres in one anuvāka. 10.1.1–10.1.4 are mostly triṣṭubh lines printed two pādas to a line, counted 20–25 syllables (10.1.1: 22, 23, 22, 21, 25, 21, 22, 22, 22, 22), with the pratīka line in 10.1.3 (13) outside the metre and anuṣṭubh lines in 10.1.2 (15–19). The gāyatrīs are 8 + 8 + 8 in principle but are printed across lines and vary (16 and 8, 17 and 9). The bath mantras are mainly anuṣṭubh lines of 16; the anonymous commentator calls the verse mṛttike hana … a six-pāda mahāpaṅkti («षट्पादेयमृङ्महापङ्क्तिच्छन्दस्का»), where Bhāskara counts mṛttike hana as an anuṣṭubh («मृत्तिके हनेति तृतीया अनुष्टुप्»). The Ṛgvedic verses in 10.1.9–10.1.11 and 10.1.15 are triṣṭubh (20–23); 10.1.15 opens with short prose formulas (8–11).

beginner: This is the longest section of the Mahānārāyaṇa, and it has three parts. The first is a hymn about the one who lies beyond the ocean of the world and yet moves within it: all the gods rest in him, time itself is born from him, and no eye can see him, only the heart. Those who know him, the text says, become immortal. The second part is a row of short prayers in the same shape as the famous gāyatrī verse: ‘we know this god, we meditate on him, may he move us’, addressed in turn to Rudra, Gaṇeśa, Nandin, Skanda, Garuḍa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Narasiṃha, the Sun, Agni and Durgā. The third part is the set of mantras the old commentators assign to the ritual bath: words said over grass and earth, while standing in the water, while under it, and while sipping water afterwards. It ends with the bather saying, ‘I am light; I am brahman.’
analogy: Like a river that rises in the mountains and reaches the bathing steps of a village: the same water is first described from far off as the source of everything, then called by many local names, then simply stepped into.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Three groups of mantras. 10.1.1–10.1.4: a hymn to the one ‘beyond the waters’, greater than the great and subtler than the subtle, in whom the world gathers and disperses, from whom time is born, whom no one has grasped and whom only the heart sees; two pratīkas point to passages recited at that place. 10.1.4–10.1.5: prayers to Agni and to the lord of the seat. 10.1.5–10.1.7: twelve gāyatrīs, to Rudra (twice), the tusked one, Nandin, the six-faced one, Garuḍa, Brahman, Viṣṇu, Narasiṃha, Āditya, Agni and Durgā. 10.1.7–10.1.15: mantras over dūrvā grass and earth, to Indra and the waters, to Varuṇa, to the rivers, the aghamarṣaṇa hymn ‘ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca’, and the self-statements ‘I am brahman’.

commentary.q: How do the commentators divide it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator closes the first part with «तदेवं ब्रह्मविद्या प्रतिपादिता», the second with «एवं द्वादश गायत्र्यो व्याख्याताः», and opens the third with «अथ स्नानाङ्गभूता मन्त्र उच्यन्ते». Sāyaṇa likewise says the knowledge of brahman is taught here from ambhasy apāre onward: «एवमत्राप्यम्भस्य पार इत्यादिना ब्रह्मतत्त्वमभिहितम्».

commentary.q: What do the pratīkas in 10.1.3 point to?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The line adbhyas sambhūto hiraṇyagarbha ityaṣṭau names two passages by their opening words. The anonymous commentator says they are quoted from elsewhere to confirm what was just said («उक्तार्थदार्ढ्याय प्रदेशान्तरपठितान्मन्त्रानुदाहरति»): the anuvāka beginning adbhyaḥ sambhūtaḥ, in which the knower of the highest is said to be free of death («तस्मिन्ननुवाके तमेवं विद्वानमृत इह भवतीति परमात्मतत्त्वविदो मरणराहित्यमुक्तम्»), and the eight verses beginning hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre, found in the fourth book, first chapter, of the Saṃhitā («संहितायाश्चतुर्थकाण्डे प्रथमप्रपाठके»). The Ānandāśrama and Tirupati texts write both passages out in full; the base keeps the pratīka.

commentary.q: Who are the gāyatrīs addressed to?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator counts twelve and names the deity of each; he begins with Rudra in his universal form («तत्राऽऽदौ विश्वरूपधरं रुद्रं प्रार्थयते»), explains the tusked one as Vināyaka, the one with the discus-like mouth as Nandikeśvara, and the commander of the great army as the six-faced god («महती देवसेना यस्य तस्मै»). Sāyaṇa, following the Drāviḍa text, explains six («तत्र षड्भिर्गायत्रीभिरात्मप्राप्तिद्वारभूता देवताविशेषाः प्रार्थ्यन्ते»); Bhāskara counts five beginning with tatpuruṣāya («तत्पुरुषायेत्याद्याः पञ्च गायत्र्यः») and then further gāyatrīs for Vighneśvara and others («अथ प्रसङ्गाद् विघ्नेश्वराद्याराधनार्था गायत्र्य आम्नाताः»). The number of gāyatrīs is a difference of recension.

commentary.q: How are the bath mantras used?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator assigns each group to a step of the bath. The dūrvā verses are said while placing dūrvā grass with earth on the head («शिरसि मृत्तिकया सह दूर्वां धारयितुं दूर्वाभिमन्त्रणमन्त्रानाह»); Bhāskara calls the earth verses the mantras for taking earth at the time of bathing («स्नानकाले मृद्ग्रहणमन्त्राः»). Standing knee-deep («जानुदघ्ने जले प्रविश्य जप्यौ मन्त्रावाह»), then navel-deep («नाभिद्वयसजले स्थित्वा जप्यान्मन्त्रानाह»); the rivers are invoked as places of bathing («तीर्थभूतानां गङ्गादीनामावाहनमन्त्रमाह»); the aghamarṣaṇa is said under water with breath restraint («जले निमग्नस्य प्राणायामार्थमघमर्षणसूक्तमाह»); then three verses for immersion («अघमर्षणं कृत्वाऽत ऊर्ध्वमवगाहनार्था ऋचो दर्शयति»); then the sipping after the bath («स्नातवतः पुरुषस्याऽऽचमनमन्त्रानाह»); and a further bath for hidden wrongs («रहस्यपापाक्षयार्थे स्नानमन्त्रमाह»). Bhāskara agrees on the order after the aghamarṣaṇa («अघमर्षणोत्तरकालम् उत्तराभिस्तिसृभिः स्नायात्»). This is the commentators’ account of the rite; the text itself does not describe the actions.

commentary.q: What are ṛta and satya in the aghamarṣaṇa?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator explains ṛta as the five elements and satya as the world they make, both ‘true until knowledge dawns’; he records another view: «केचित्तु ऋतं यथार्थभाषणं सत्यं यथार्थं संकल्पनमिति व्याचक्षते», that ṛta is speaking truly and satya is intending truly, and objects that on that view the creation of the elements must be supplied.

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: A subjunctive (leṭ) form of pra-√cud, ‘may he impel’. Bhāskara: «प्रचोदयात् प्रचोदयतु वर्तयतु लेट्याडागमः» — the augment ā of the subjunctive, glossed by the imperative. The anonymous commentator notes that in all these gāyatrīs gender and case are freely interchanged («सर्वत्र गायत्रीमन्त्रेषु बहुलं लिङ्गादिव्यत्ययः»), so tatpuruṣāya, a dative, is read as an accusative.

commentary.q: Why do the witnesses differ so much here?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa warns that from this point the readings of the different regions differ greatly («इत ऊर्ध्वं तेषु तेषु देशेषु श्रुतिपाठा अत्यन्तविलक्षणाः») and says he follows the Drāviḍa text («द्राविडपाठस्याऽऽदृतत्वाद्वयमपि तमेवाऽऽदृत्य व्याख्यास्यामः»). The anonymous commentator records three arrangements of the whole text, of 64, 74 and 80 anuvākas («तत्र द्राविडानां चतुःषष्ठ्यनुवाकक्रमपाठः»). In this anuvāka the Ānandāśrama text opens with harih om, writes out the two pratīka passages, reads nandiḥ where the base has ṣaṇmukhaḥ in the line after mahāsenāya, and adds an index line which names the twelve gāyatrī deities in order, Nandin and Ṣaṇmukha both among them; the Tirupati text adds gāyatryāḥ, writes out the pratīkas, and omits kārya in akāryakārī and the final induḥ.

advaita.text: Both commentators read the hymn as teaching that the world seen as many through ignorance is, seen by knowledge, brahman alone («यद्यज्जगदविद्यादृष्ट्या नानाविधं प्रतीयते तत्सर्वं विद्यादृष्ट्याऽखण्डैकरसं ब्रह्मैव»). On the bather’s words ‘I am brahman’ they say nothing new is gained: individuality had only been superimposed on brahman through ignorance («वस्तुतो ब्रह्मण्येव मयि पूर्वमज्ञानाज्जीवत्वमारोपितमासीत्»), «न तु नूतनं किंचिद्ब्रह्मत्वमागतम्». The anonymous commentator also says the knower of brahman becomes brahman («ब्रह्मविद्ब्रह्मैव भवति»).

schools.disagreement: The Advaita reading is stated by the two commentators present, both of whom are Advaitins (the anonymous commentator opens by honouring Śaṅkara, «आचार्यं शंकरं भजे»). No Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources; Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here. Bhāskara’s comment on this anuvāka, as far as it survives in the copy used, is grammatical and ritual and states no school position.

parallels.quote: न सन्दृशे तिष्ठति रूपमस्य न चक्षुषा पश्यति कश्चनैनम्
parallels.note: The first verse of 10.1.3 is the Kaṭha’s verse almost word for word; the Kaṭha reads ya etad vidur where the Mahānārāyaṇa reads ya enaṃ viduḥ.

The anonymous commentator cites the Gārgī dialogue on akṣare parame vyoman (10.1.1): the unmanifest, on which the world is woven, rests in the imperishable. 10.1.3 uses the same pair of words, sa otaḥ protaś ca.
The bather’s brahmāham asmi (10.1.15) repeats the Bṛhadāraṇyaka’s words. The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read it there as the recognition of what one already is, not a new state gained.
The Ṛgveda verse to the earth quoted in 10.1.10; the Ṛgveda text joins bhavānṛkṣarā, which the anonymous commentator divides bhavā nṛkṣarā.
The svasti verse in 10.1.9 is this Ṛgveda verse; the Taittirīya text writes the sibilant doubled before s (vṛddhaśravās svasti).

contemporary.text: The anuvāka sets a vast hymn about the source of everything beside the plain steps of washing: grass, earth, knee-deep water, a sip from the hand. The commentators hold the two together: the bath is where the hymn is put into practice, and its last words are ‘I am brahman’. One modern way to read this is that large ideas need small, repeated acts to live in, and small acts need a large idea to be more than habit. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: The hymn says the highest is seen not by the eye but by the heart. What in your own experience is known that way?
reflect.deeper: Why might a text place a hymn to the source of all things directly before the mantras of an ordinary daily bath?
reflect.practice: The next time you wash, do it slowly and attentively, as a thing done on purpose rather than in a hurry.

references.text: The pratīka adbhyas sambhūto hiraṇyagarbha ityaṣṭau points, by the anonymous commentator’s account, to the anuvāka adbhyaḥ sambhūtaḥ, recited among the mantras of the fire-altar, and to the eight verses hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre of the Saṃhitā, fourth book, first chapter; they are not reproduced in the base, and the record does not supply them.

Other Ṛgvedic verses in this anuvāka, noted but not imported (the importer reads only maṇḍala 1): imaṃ me gaṅge (the river hymn), the aghamarṣaṇa ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca, āpo hi ṣṭhā, ā krān samudraḥ and vṛṣā pavitre adhi sāno avye; brahma jajñānam is a verse of the Yajurveda Saṃhitās.

Sāyaṇa’s anuvāka 1 and Bhāskara’s anuvāka 1 cover this anuvāka and continue into the Durgā hymn (jātavedase …), which the base prints as 10.2. Bhāskara’s comment in the copy used begins at pra tad voce (10.1.3); his comment on 10.1.1–10.1.2 is not in it.

flags.note: At 10.1.6 the Ānandāśrama and Tirupati texts read nandiḥ where the base reads ṣaṇmukhaḥ after mahāsenāya (corrections.json, review). The anonymous commentator explains a gāyatrī to the six-faced commander of the army there, which supports the base, and the Ānandāśrama text’s own index line names both Nandin and Ṣaṇmukha among the twelve; the printed sources should still be checked.
The two pratīka passages in 10.1.3 are written out in full by AP and T (corrections.json, review); the base keeps the pratīka, and the record explains them only as the anonymous commentator does.

The padaccheda rejoins only with an extended sandhi engine: the Taittirīya spellings ग्श्/ग्स्, n + s → nts, Vedic -āṃ before a vowel, Vedic -aḥ + a → -o a, ऱ and a comma in the base. The engine change is reported, not made.

lālīlāya (10.1.7) and the epithets āpānta-manyu, tṛpala-prabharmā (10.1.9) are rare words; the glosses of lālīlāya follow the anonymous commentator, and his explanation of the two Ṛgvedic epithets is damaged in the copy used, so their meanings are marked uncertain.
The negative in ‘do not make me weep’ (10.1.15) and the reading nṛkṣarā (10.1.10) follow the anonymous commentator; the Śaiva reading of soma as sa-umā is reported as his.
The number of gāyatrīs differs by recension: twelve in the base and the anonymous commentary, six explained by Sāyaṇa, five named by Bhāskara before further ones.
